intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal dominant distal hereditary motor neuronopathy-14 (HMND14), also called distal hereditary motor neuronopathy type VIIB (HMN7B), is caused by heterozygous mutation in the dynactin gene (DCTN1; 601143) on chromosome 2p13.

checks.explanation: not supported by any of the 2 cited papers. Disease nomenclature (HMND14/HMN7B) is not in the abstract.

checks.claim: HMND14 is caused by heterozygous mutation in the dynactin gene DCTN1.
checks.evidence_quote: Mutation analysis of a gene in this interval that encodes the largest subunit of the axonal transport protein dynactin showed a single base-pair change resulting in an amino-acid substitution
checks.explanation: Abstract supports a dynactin gene mutation causing lower motor neuron disease, but heterozygosity and the dominant inheritance are not stated in the abstract.

checks.claim: The DCTN1 gene is located on chromosome 2p13.
checks.evidence_quote: Here we show linkage of a lower motor neuron disease to a region of 4 Mb at chromosome 2p13. Mutation analysis of a gene in this interval that encodes the largest subunit of the axonal transport protein dynactin
checks.explanation: The dynactin gene lies in the 2p13 interval.

paragraphs.text: Autosomal dominant distal hereditary motor neuronopathy-14 is a slowly progressive lower motor neuron disease. It begins in adulthood with breathing difficulty caused by vocal fold paralysis. Later features include weakness of the face and weakness and atrophy of distal muscles, most notably in the hands. Sensation is spared.

checks.explanation: The abstract calls it a lower motor neuron disease; 'slowly progressive' is not stated in the abstract.

paragraphs.text: Puls et al. (2003) studied a large North American kindred with an autosomal dominant lower motor neuron disorder. Affected members first had breathing difficulty from bilateral vocal fold paralysis. Weakness of the face and weakness and atrophy of the hand muscles followed, and the disease later reached the distal lower limbs. Sensation was normal, and there were no signs of upper motor neuron involvement.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of the kindred with lower motor neuron disease and vocal fold paralysis, Puls et al. (2003) found a heterozygous gly59-to-ser (G59S) mutation in the DCTN1 gene, which encodes the p150(Glued) subunit of dynactin. The mutation lies in the highly conserved CAP-Gly microtubule-binding domain. It segregated with the disease. Functional studies showed that the mutant protein bound microtubules less well than normal, and that the mutant protein formed aggregates in cultured cells. The authors proposed that the mutation disrupts dynein/dynactin-dependent axonal transport in motor neurons.

checks.evidence_quote: showed a single base-pair change resulting in an amino-acid substitution that is predicted to distort the folding of dynactin's microtubule-binding domain
checks.explanation: A missense change is reported, but the abstract does not specify G59S, heterozygosity or vocal fold paralysis.

checks.explanation: The gist matches, but the abstract does not specifically mention dynein or say the mutation disrupts axonal transport in motor neurons.

paragraphs.text: Other mutations in the CAP-Gly domain of DCTN1 cause Perry syndrome, a different disorder with parkinsonism, depression, weight loss, and central hypoventilation (Farrer et al., 2009). Unlike G59S, these mutations did not appear to cause the same distal motor neuron phenotype.
